case_study_insert.main_stem: Varden Block Materials (VBM) is a partnership in the construction-materials sector, employing a workforce of 40 near Leeds. Founded in 2013 by partners Ellis Varden and Ruth Pike, the business makes concrete paving blocks for housebuilders and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. VBM plans to invest $720,000 in an automated block-moulding press with a water-recycling system, financed by a $420,000 hire purchase agreement and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.40 a unit and a selling price of $12.40, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. VBM faces two problems: a waste rate of 6.8% from off-cut concrete and frequent quality complaints from builders.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Waste Report — Q4 2025: The moulding line produced 20,000 paving blocks last quarter; 6.8% were scrapped as off-cuts, down from 9.2% in the previous quarter. Builder complaints about chipped edges fell from 36 to 17 per month. Average delivery time is 3.8 days. A survey of 380 small builders found that 63% would pay up to $0.45 more for water-recycled blocks, and 55% check environmental credentials when choosing suppliers. Water use per 1,000 blocks is 4,800 litres. The plant manager is comparing end-of-line quality control inspection with quality assurance based on prevention and team working.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Varden Block Materials for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Construction Bulletin (March 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.75%, increasing the cost of variable-rate borrowing and hire purchase finance. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $12.90 to $13.73 per hour from April 2026. (3) Cement and aggregate input costs have increased 10.5% year-on-year, while construction cost inflation is 5.9% and regional house-building output grew 2.6% over the same period.

questions.question_text: VBM is funding its $720,000 block press through a $420,000 hire purchase agreement. Explain two advantages for VBM of using retained profit for the $300,000 portion instead of more hire purchase finance.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit does not add another fixed repayment obligation, so the partnership avoids increasing the instalments already due under the $420,000 hire purchase agreement. With fixed costs of $240,000 a year and a 6.8% waste rate to tackle, keeping more cash inside VBM helps the partners pay for raw materials and maintain the 80,000-unit output without asking Ellis Varden and Ruth Pike to inject further personal capital.

Point 2: Using $300,000 of money already earned keeps ownership and control with the two partners rather than tying more of the firm's future cash to a finance company for the automated block-moulding press. Unlike hire purchase, where the asset can be repossessed if instalments are missed, retained profit carries no such risk. That flexibility matters when 55% of surveyed builders check environmental credentials and demand for water-recycled blocks may change quickly; the partnership can redirect the saved cash into quality improvements instead of being locked into another fixed contract.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over hire purchase identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual analysis of VBM's $300,000 retained profit, hire purchase and operating costs.

questions.question_text: VBM wants to win more small-builder customers for its water-recycled blocks. Consider advertising in trade magazines, sponsorship with a builders' merchant, or search-engine advertising. Which should VBM choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade magazine advertising: A regional trade title would reach the small builders VBM already supplies and allow technical details of the water-recycling system to be shown, which matters because 55% of the 380 surveyed builders check environmental credentials. It is inexpensive for a 40-person partnership. However, readership is falling, response is slow and hard to measure, and many readers are outside the Leeds delivery area, so it cannot readily fill the capacity of the $720,000 press.

Builders' merchant sponsorship: Paying a merchant to display water-recycled blocks puts the product where builders buy materials and can drive immediate orders, helped by the 63% who would pay $0.45 more. The merchant's staff can recommend the blocks at the point of sale. The drawbacks are that the sponsor controls the display, the deal is a recurring cost alongside $240,000 of fixed costs, and chipped-edge complaints of 17 a month could damage trust if quality is not fixed first.

Search-engine advertising: Paid search reaches builders at the moment they look for paving blocks, can be targeted at Leeds and surrounding towns, and produces measurable clicks and enquiries at a controllable budget. It also promotes the 4,800 litres of water saved per 1,000 blocks. Its weakness is that clicks are cheap but loyalty is low, and many searchers are price-focused rather than attracted by environmental credentials.

Recommendation: VBM should choose search-engine advertising, supported later by a small merchant display. Search is rejected as a complete answer only because it builds little loyalty, but it wins now on cost, measurability and local targeting; trade magazines are rejected as slow and unfocused, and full merchant sponsorship is rejected as an ongoing expense that hands too much control to another business while the 6.8% waste rate is still being reduced.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Lists the promotional options with little reference to VBM's customers or product.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of VBM.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options and recommends one with clear reasons for rejecting trade magazines and sponsorship.

questions.question_text: VBM's waste rate is 6.8% and builder complaints are rising. Explain two benefits for VBM of using laissez-faire leadership together with quality circles in its moulding team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives experienced moulding operators freedom to decide how to reduce the 6.8% off-cut waste, and quality circles let them meet regularly to share practical solutions. Because the people running the press know where chipped edges occur, their ideas can cut scrap faster than instructions from the partners, helping VBM protect the 20,000 blocks made each quarter and reduce the 36 to 17 monthly complaints trend further.

Point 2: Being trusted to solve problems raises job satisfaction and motivation, which suits the flat structure and helps retain skilled staff in a workforce of 40 with a laissez-faire style. Higher involvement supports the team working that the manager is already comparing with quality assurance, and it avoids spending on outside expertise while the partnership services $420,000 of hire purchase. If operators own the improvement, the 9.2% waste figure of the previous quarter is more likely to keep falling without close supervision.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of laissez-faire leadership or quality circles identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for analysis applied to VBM's waste, complaints, flat structure and workforce.

questions.question_text: VBM must cut its 6.8% waste rate. Consider end-of-line quality control inspection or quality assurance through prevention and team working. Which should VBM choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Quality control inspection: Checking finished blocks at the end of the line would catch chipped edges before they reach the 380 small builders, directly addressing the 17 complaints a month. It gives clear pass/fail data and is easy to organise in a 40-person plant. However, it only finds waste after materials and machine time have been used, so it does not reduce the 6.8% scrap rate itself; inspectors add labour cost, and rejected blocks still have to be disposed of, which conflicts with saving 4,800 litres of water per 1,000 blocks.

Quality assurance: Building quality in through prevention, supplier checks on aggregates and team working attacks the causes of chipped edges, such as mould wear and mixing errors. The report already shows waste falling from 9.2% to 6.8%, so prevention has worked here. It also suits the flat structure and laissez-faire leadership because operators can stop the press when settings drift. Its limitations are that it takes time to train staff, needs accurate records, and cannot replace a final check for every block during the first weeks of the new $720,000 press.

Decision: VBM should choose quality assurance through prevention and team working, retaining a light final check only during commissioning. Quality control is rejected as the main method because it detects rather than prevents the 6.8% waste and keeps paying for scrap; quality assurance wins because it removes the cause of complaints, protects the 4,800-litre water saving and makes better use of the workforce of 40 than a separate inspection team.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes inspection and prevention with little application to VBM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses both approaches using VBM's waste, complaint and water figures.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Fully evaluates both approaches and reaches a justified decision that rejects the alternative.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how VBM's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $240,000 ÷ ($12.40 − $7.40) = $240,000 ÷ $5.00 = 48,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 48,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $12.40 − $7.40 = $5.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $5.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways VBM's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 48,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 80,000 units: the margin of safety is 32,000 units, so VBM knows how far housebuilder demand could fall before the $720,000 press stops covering its $240,000 fixed costs.
2. Test the survey result that 63% of builders would pay $0.45 more: a price of $12.85 would lift contribution to $5.45, worth 80,000 × $0.45 = $36,000 a year if the premium were achieved on all blocks.
3. Check affordability of the press: at 80,000 units total contribution is 80,000 × $5.00 = $400,000, leaving $160,000 after fixed costs to meet the $420,000 hire purchase instalments and the $28,000 interest recorded in Appendix 2.
4. Benchmark with average total cost of $10.40 ($240,000 ÷ 80,000 + $7.40) and labour productivity of 80,000 ÷ 40 = 2,000 units per worker, so the partners can judge whether the 6.8% waste rate is pushing cost per block above that benchmark.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 48,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $5.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 32,000-unit margin of safety; $0.45 premium worth $36,000; total contribution of $400,000 for hire purchase planning; and cost benchmarking at $10.40 with 2,000 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in each of (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each of four valid applied uses in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VBM's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has VBM's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 12.5%
ROCE 2024 = 12.5%
ROCE 2025 = 15.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit = $1,000,000 revenue − $600,000 cost of sales = $400,000; 2025 gross profit = $1,200,000 − $660,000 = $540,000. For 2024, $400,000 ÷ $1,000,000 = 0.400; $100,000 operating profit ÷ $1,000,000 = 0.100; $100,000 ÷ $800,000 capital employed = 0.125. For 2025, $540,000 ÷ $1,200,000 = 0.450; $150,000 ÷ $1,200,000 = 0.125; $150,000 ÷ $1,000,000 = 0.150.

Evaluation: Revenue rose by 20.0%, from $1,000,000 to $1,200,000, while cost of sales increased by only $60,000, so gross profit grew from $400,000 to $540,000. This is consistent with the survey evidence that 63% of builders would pay $0.45 more for water-recycled blocks, and it suggests that the partnership is capturing better prices on its paving blocks. Operating profit rose by half, from $100,000 to $150,000, showing that the $240,000 fixed costs were spread over more output despite the 6.8% waste rate. ROCE improved from 12.5% to 15.0% even though capital employed grew from $800,000 to $1,000,000 to fund the new press, which is encouraging for the two partners. Interest payable increased from $20,000 to $28,000, so the $420,000 hire purchase commitment does take part of the benefit, but it remains small next to $150,000 of operating profit.

Conclusion: VBM's profitability has improved on every measure. Gross margin moved from 40.0% to 45.0%, operating margin from 10.0% to 12.5% and ROCE from 12.5% to 15.0%, and the rise in returns was achieved while the asset base expanded. The main caution is the growing interest charge, but the $720,000 investment is currently supporting higher rather than lower returns.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Quotes individual Appendix 2 figures with little calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates the three ratios for both years and describes the trend with some VBM context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratios for both years plus evaluation of revenue, costs, capital employed, interest and a justified conclusion.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VBM of installing a water-recycling system on its block-moulding press.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The operations report shows water use of 4,800 litres per 1,000 blocks, so recycling water cuts both the amount VBM draws and the waste it discharges, supporting the 55% of surveyed builders who check environmental credentials. It also reduces exposure to water restrictions and complements the 63% who would pay $0.45 more, helping protect the 45.0% gross margin and the $720,000 investment in the new press.

Disadvantage: A water-recycling system adds to the capital cost of the $720,000 press and needs maintenance, which could raise the $7.40 variable cost or the $240,000 fixed costs if filters and pumps are serviced often. If the system breaks down, the 6.8% waste rate could worsen because dry mixes produce chipped blocks, adding to the 17 monthly complaints. The environmental benefit only pays if builders actually accept the $0.45 premium across all 80,000 units, which the survey of 380 small builders does not guarantee, so VBM should pilot the system and monitor the 6.8% waste rate before committing further funds.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for development with VBM's water, survey, cost and waste figures.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 10.5% rise in cement and aggregate costs will affect VBM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.75%): The bulletin says the change raises the cost of hire purchase finance as well as variable-rate borrowing. If VBM's $420,000 hire purchase agreement tracks the change, a 0.75 percentage point increase would add 0.0075 × $420,000 = $3,150 a year. That is noticeable but still modest beside fixed costs of $240,000 and operating profit of $150,000, and the $300,000 of retained profit used for the press reduces the amount exposed. VBM can also limit the damage by agreeing a fixed rate on future finance.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, from $12.90 to $13.73 an hour): With a workforce of 40, higher pay for eligible staff raises the cost of running the moulding line and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual wages, so an annual wage bill cannot be calculated fairly. The supported comparison is productivity of 80,000 units ÷ 40 workers = 2,000 units per worker; if the 6.8% waste rate falls and that productivity is maintained, the extra wage cost is spread over 2,000 blocks per worker. If output slips, unit labour cost rises and the $5.00 contribution per unit shrinks. This is a real pressure but one VBM can influence through team working and prevention.

Input-cost inflation (10.5% on cement and aggregate): The insert gives a variable cost of $7.40 per unit but never breaks it into components, so only a bound can be shown: if the whole variable cost were exposed, 10.5% × $7.40 = about $0.78 per unit, and at 80,000 units that is roughly $62,160 a year (80,000 × $0.777). Even a smaller exposed share would cut contribution substantially, and higher cement prices also threaten the 45.0% gross margin. The $0.45 premium may recover only part of this because the 380 surveyed builders are small and price-sensitive.

Conclusion: The 10.5% rise in cement and aggregate costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every block, could remove about $62,160 of contribution annually on the stated bound, and directly erodes the margin that justifies the $720,000 press. The interest rise adds around $3,150 and can be fixed in future deals, while the wage rise can be offset by holding 2,000 units per worker, so neither matches the reach and persistence of input-cost inflation.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three changes with limited application to VBM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses at least two changes with correct VBM figures and some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes in context using only insert-derived arithmetic and reaches a justified greatest-impact conclusion.
